name: Mandarin
note: Pinyin only — learning to speak, not to read characters.

alphabet.e: j in jar, tongue curled back
ch in chart, tongue curled back
sh in shirt, tongue curled back
r in rue, tongue curled back
j in jeep, tongue flat and forward
ch in cheap, with a puff of air
sh in sheep, tongue flat and forward
ts in cats, with a puff of air
after z, c, s: a buzzing held vowel

units.title: BASICS
units.subtitle: Greet people, name who is who, and count to ten

tips.b: Every full syllable carries one of four pitch shapes, and the shape is part of the word. The mark over the vowel gives it: level, rising, dipping, falling.
A syllable written without a tone mark is neutral: short, light, and pitched by the syllable in front of it. The second half of a doubled word is neutral, as in xièxie.
When two third tones meet, the first is said as a second tone. The spelling keeps both third-tone marks, so nǐ hǎo is written with two and spoken as ní hǎo.

tips.h: One spoken word for he and she
tips.b: Mandarin says tā for he, she and it. The characters differ, 他 for a man and 她 for a woman, but the sound is one word, so context carries the difference.
The neutral-tone syllable men turns a pronoun into its plural: wǒ becomes wǒmen. Nouns keep one form for one and for many, so rén covers person and people alike.

tips.h: shì links a noun to a noun
tips.b: The verb shì joins two nouns and never changes for person or number: wǒ shì, tā shì, wǒmen shì. Before an adjective Mandarin uses hěn instead, so wǒ hěn hǎo carries no shì.

tips.h: Answering without a word for yes
tips.b: Mandarin answers a question by giving the verb back, positive or negative. To a question with shì the answer is shì or bú shì; to a question about being right it is duì or bú duì.

tips.h: yě and dōu sit before the verb
tips.b: An adverb such as yě or dōu stands between the subject and the verb, never at the end of the sentence. Both may appear together, in that order: yě dōu.

phrases.e: excuse me, are you the teacher

tips.h: Every count needs a measure word
tips.b: A number never attaches straight to a noun. A measure word stands between them, and gè is the general one that fits most nouns: sān gè rén, three people.
Numbers above ten are built from ten: shíyī is ten-one, èrshí is two-ten, èrshíwǔ is two-ten-five. Nothing in the pattern is irregular.
In counting, yī keeps its first tone. Standing before a noun it changes: before a fourth tone it becomes yí, and before any other tone it becomes yì. Pinyin writes the change.

phrases.t: wǒ jiā yǒu sì gè rén
phrases.e: there are four people in my family
phrases.ipa: u̯ɔ²¹⁴ tɕi̯a⁵ i̯ou̯²¹⁴ sɹ̩⁵¹ kɤ⁵¹ ʐən³⁵

units.title: EVERYDAY
units.subtitle: Food, drink, colour, and the people at home

tips.b: Mandarin verbs do not change for person, number or tense: wǒ chī, tā chī, wǒmen chī. Time is given by a time word such as jīntiān, not by the verb.
An adjective is its own predicate, so shì does not appear before it. The adverb hěn holds the slot instead and is much weaker than the English very.
Measure words are chosen by what is counted. A served drink takes bēi, not the general gè: yì bēi chá, sān bēi shuǐ.
The negative bù is fourth tone, and before another fourth tone it rises to bú. Pinyin writes the change: bù hē, bú shì, bú kèqi.

phrases.e: I drink a cup of tea

tips.h: de ties a modifier to its noun
tips.b: The particle de attaches a describing word to the noun that follows it: hóngsè de píngguǒ. The same de marks possession, standing between owner and thing: wǒ de chá.
The bare syllable hóng or lán works straight in front of a noun. Adding sè makes it the name of the colour, which is the form used after shì and before de.

phrases.t: wǒ yǒu yí gè huángsè de bēizi
phrases.ipa: u̯ɔ²¹⁴ i̯ou̯²¹⁴ i³⁵ kɤ⁵¹ xu̯ɑŋ³⁵.sɤ⁵¹ tə pei̯⁵.tsɹ̩

tips.h: de is dropped for close family
tips.b: Possession normally takes de, but a family member or a close relation is said without it: wǒ māma, tā gēge. A thing keeps the de: wǒ de chá.
Mandarin has no plain word for brother or sister. The older and the younger one are separate words: gēge and dìdi, jiějie and mèimei.

phrases.t: bàba hé māma dōu shì lǎoshī
phrases.e: dad and mum are both teachers
phrases.ipa: pa⁵¹.pa xɤ³⁵ ma⁵.ma tou̯⁵ ʂʐ̩⁵¹ lɑu̯²¹⁴.ʂʐ̩⁵

units.title: ACTIONS
units.subtitle: Say what people do, describe it, ask about it, and deny it

tips.b: The basic order matches English: wǒ chī fàn. Mandarin has no articles, so fàn covers rice, the rice and some rice, and nothing marks the noun as singular or plural.
A verb that takes another verb is followed by it directly, with no particle between them. English to has no equivalent here.

tips.h: yǒu for having and for there is
tips.b: yǒu covers possession and existence alike. With a person in front it is has; with a place in front it states what is there.
eg: there are four people at home

tips.b: A bare adjective after a noun reads as a comparison: chá hǎo suggests the tea is better than something else. hěn fills the slot and carries almost none of its literal force.
eg: there is a lot of rice

tips.b: Used as a modifier the adjective stands in front of the noun. One syllable attaches directly; two syllables take de between them.

phrases.t: wǒ jiā de rén bù duō
phrases.ipa: u̯ɔ²¹⁴ tɕi̯a⁵ tə ʐən³⁵ pu⁵¹ tu̯ɔ⁵
phrases.lit: my home DE people not many

tips.h: A question word keeps its place
tips.b: Mandarin leaves the question word where the answer belongs, so the question and its answer have the same word order.
Adding ma to the end of a statement turns it into a question and changes nothing else. A sentence that already carries a question word takes no ma.
A second way to ask is to say the verb, then its negative: shì bu shì, hǎo bu hǎo. It carries the same meaning as ma and takes no ma.

phrases.e: how many children do you have
why does he not eat meat

tips.h: bù and méi divide the work
tips.b: bù denies the present, the habitual and the future: tā bù chī ròu. méi denies that something happened: tā méi chī fàn.

tips.h: yǒu is negated only by méi
tips.b: The verb yǒu never takes bù. Its negative is méiyǒu, which shortens to méi in front of another verb.
bié in front of a verb tells someone not to do it. búyòng says the action is unnecessary rather than unwanted.

phrases.e: I do not have an older sister

phrases.t: wǒ xǐhuan chá, dànshì bù xǐhuan kāfēi
phrases.e: I like tea but not coffee
phrases.ipa: u̯ɔ²¹⁴ ɕi²¹⁴.xu̯an tʂʰa³⁵ tan⁵¹.ʂʐ̩⁵¹ pu⁵¹ ɕi²¹⁴.xu̯an kʰa⁵.fei̯⁵
phrases.note: 我喜欢茶但是不喜欢咖啡

units.title: AT HOME
units.subtitle: The rooms of a house, what stands in them, clothes and animals

tips.h: zài places a person or a thing
tips.b: zài states where something is and needs no other verb: wǒ zài jiā. The place always follows zài, and the whole group stands after the subject.
A where question puts nǎr in the place slot, and the answer replaces nǎr with the place. No other word moves.
A flat-topped thing is counted with zhāng, a thing held by a handle with bǎ. The measure word is fixed by the noun, not chosen freely.

tips.h: zhè and nà need a measure word
tips.b: This and that behave like numbers: a measure word stands between them and the noun. zhè gè rén, nà běn shū.
de after a question word builds the possessive, and the phrase stays where the answer would stand.
chuān is used for what the body goes into: clothes and shoes. dài is used for what is put on: a hat, glasses, a watch.
jiàn counts a garment for the upper body, tiáo counts a long one such as trousers or a skirt, and shuāng counts what comes in pairs.

phrases.t: tā de xiézi shì hēisè de
phrases.ipa: tʰa⁵ tə ɕi̯ɛ³⁵.tsɹ̩ ʂʐ̩⁵¹ xei̯⁵.sɤ⁵¹ tə

phrases.e: I have three pairs of socks

tips.b: The measure word for an animal is usually zhī: yì zhī gǒu, sān zhī māo. A horse takes pǐ and a fish takes tiáo.

tips.h: A noun counts as one or as many
tips.b: gǒu is dog and dogs alike; nothing is added for the plural. Number comes from the count phrase in front of the noun.

phrases.t: tā jiā yǒu sān zhī māo
phrases.e: there are three cats at his home
phrases.ipa: tʰa⁵ tɕi̯a⁵ i̯ou̯²¹⁴ san⁵ tʂʐ̩⁵ mɑu̯⁵

phrases.t: niǎo hěn xiǎo, mǎ hěn dà
phrases.e: birds are small, horses are big
phrases.ipa: ni̯ɑu̯²¹⁴ xən²¹⁴ ɕi̯ɑu̯²¹⁴ ma²¹⁴ xən²¹⁴ ta⁵¹

units.title: TIME
units.subtitle: The week, the calendar, the clock and the weather

tips.h: A time word comes before the verb
tips.b: A time expression stands at the head of the sentence or straight after the subject, and never after the verb: míngtiān wǒ qù, or wǒ míngtiān qù.

tips.h: The days of the week are numbered
tips.b: xīngqī plus a number gives the day, counting from Monday as one. Sunday breaks the count and is xīngqītiān.

tips.h: The verb does not mark the past
tips.b: zuótiān wǒ chī fàn is yesterday I ate. The time word places the action, and the verb keeps the one form it has.

phrases.e: tomorrow I go to your home
what do you do at the weekend

tips.h: Months are a number plus yuè
tips.b: No month carries a name of its own: yīyuè is month one, shí'èryuè is month twelve. The same yuè is the word for month itself.

tips.h: Dates run from large to small
tips.b: A date names the year, then the month, then the day: wǔyuè sì hào. Every Mandarin time expression narrows in the same direction.

phrases.e: today is the fourth of May

phrases.t: yī nián yǒu shí'èr gè yuè
phrases.ipa: i⁵ ni̯ɛn³⁵ i̯ou̯²¹⁴ ʂʐ̩³⁵.ɑɻ⁵¹ kɤ⁵¹ ɥɛ⁵¹

phrases.t: nǐ de shēngrì shì jǐ hào
phrases.ipa: ni²¹⁴ tə ʂəŋ⁵.ʐʐ̩⁵¹ ʂʐ̩⁵¹ tɕi²¹⁴ xɑu̯⁵¹

tips.b: The hour is a number plus diǎn, and minutes follow it: sān diǎn shí fēn. bàn after diǎn gives half past.
A Mandarin sentence sets the frame before the action: subject, time, place, verb. English puts both at the end, which reverses the order.
eg: wǒ wǎnshang zài jiā chī fàn
I eat at home in the evening

phrases.e: I get up at six every day
in the evening I am at home

tips.h: le marks a change of state
tips.b: le at the end of a sentence says the situation is new: xiàyǔ le, it has started raining. tài plus an adjective plus le says it has gone too far.
xiàyǔ and xiàxuě are complete sentences on their own, with nothing standing for the English it. Naming the weather uses tiānqì.

tips.h: The seasons are built on tiān
tips.b: Each season is a syllable plus tiān, the word for day: chūntiān, xiàtiān, qiūtiān, dōngtiān.

phrases.t: dōngtiān hěn lěng, xiàtiān hěn rè
phrases.e: winter is cold, summer is hot
phrases.ipa: tʊŋ⁵.tʰi̯ɛn⁵ xən²¹⁴ ləŋ²¹⁴ ɕi̯a⁵¹.tʰi̯ɛn⁵ xən²¹⁴ ʐɤ⁵¹

phrases.e: the weather is not very good today

units.title: GETTING AROUND
units.subtitle: Places in town, where things stand, and how to reach them

tips.h: The place stands before the verb
tips.b: A zài phrase that says where an action happens comes between the subject and the verb: wǒ zài túshūguǎn kàn shū. It cannot follow the verb.
No preposition stands between qù and the place: wǒ qù xuéxiào. The same holds for lái and for dào.

phrases.e: we go to the park in the afternoon
the food at the restaurant is delicious

tips.b: Mandarin names the object first and its position second: zhuōzi shàngmiàn is table-above. English builds the same phrase in the opposite order.
wǎng marks the direction a movement takes and stands in front of the verb: wǎng yòubian zhuǎn, wǎng qiánmiàn zǒu.

phrases.e: the book is on the table
the cat is under the chair

tips.b: zuò is used for riding inside something: a bus, a train, a plane. qí is used for what is straddled, a bicycle or a horse, and kāi is for driving.

tips.h: The means comes before the going
tips.b: Two verbs run in sequence in the order the actions happen: wǒ zuò dìtiě qù xuéxiào is take the underground, then go to school.

phrases.e: I take the underground to school

phrases.t: fēijī hěn kuài, chuán hěn màn
phrases.e: planes are fast, boats are slow
phrases.ipa: fei̯⁵.tɕi⁵ xən²¹⁴ kʰu̯ai̯⁵¹ tʂʰu̯an³⁵ xən²¹⁴ man⁵¹

phrases.e: how do you get to school

tips.h: lí measures the gap between two places
tips.b: A lí B plus an adjective states the distance: jīchǎng lí zhèlǐ hěn yuǎn. zài states position, lí states separation.
eg: the airport is far from here

tips.b: A road, a river, a fish and a pair of trousers are all counted with tiáo, the measure word for anything long and thin.

phrases.t: wǒ de hùzhào zài bāo lǐmiàn
phrases.e: my passport is in the bag
phrases.ipa: u̯ɔ²¹⁴ tə xu⁵¹.tʂɑu̯⁵¹ tsai̯⁵¹ pɑu̯⁵ li²¹⁴.mi̯ɛn⁵¹

units.title: PEOPLE
units.subtitle: Feelings, the body, being ill, and describing someone

tips.h: A feeling behaves like any adjective
tips.b: hěn holds the predicate slot in front of it, and a question is made with ma or by the A-not-A pattern: nǐ lèi bu lèi.
juéde is followed by a whole sentence, with no word standing for the English that: wǒ juéde zhōngwén hěn yǒuyìsi.

phrases.t: wǒ è le, wǒ yào chī fàn
phrases.e: I am hungry, I want to eat
phrases.ipa: u̯ɔ²¹⁴ ɤ⁵¹ lə u̯ɔ²¹⁴ i̯ɑu̯⁵¹ tʂʰʐ̩⁵ fan⁵¹

tips.h: A body part can drop de
tips.b: Possession of a body part works like family: wǒ de tóu and wǒ tóu are both said, and the shorter one is the more common in speech.
A single hand or eye is counted with zhī, and the pair with shuāng: yì shuāng shǒu, yì shuāng yǎnjing.
The part of the body comes first and téng follows it: wǒ tóu téng, tā dùzi téng. No verb for having appears in the sentence.

tips.h: le after the verb marks completion
tips.b: le right after the verb reports that the action was carried out: wǒ chī le yào. Its negative drops le and uses méi: wǒ méi chī yào.
shūfu is the state of being comfortable, and its negative is the ordinary way to report illness without naming it.

phrases.e: I do not feel well today

tips.b: A bǐ B plus an adjective states which is more: tā bǐ wǒ gāo. hěn never appears in a bǐ sentence, and the adjective takes no other change.
gēn plus yíyàng states equality, and an adjective may follow it: wǒ gēn tā yíyàng gāo. The negative is bù yíyàng.
eg: I am as tall as him

units.title: WORK AND SCHOOL
units.subtitle: The classroom, the workplace, larger numbers and money

tips.h: shàng and xià open and close a class
tips.b: shàngkè is to have a class and xiàkè is to finish one. The same pair works for a shift: shàngbān and xiàbān.
xué takes what is learned straight after it: xué zhōngwén. xuéxí names the activity and can stand alone as the whole verb.

phrases.e: the teacher is in the classroom

phrases.t: zuòyè hěn duō, yě hěn nán
phrases.e: there is a lot of homework and it is hard
phrases.ipa: tsu̯ɔ⁵¹.i̯ɛ⁵¹ xən²¹⁴ tu̯ɔ⁵ i̯ɛ²¹⁴ xən²¹⁴ nan³⁵

tips.b: huì is a skill that was learned, néng is being physically able or free to act, and kěyǐ is having permission. All three stand in front of the main verb.

tips.h: A job is stated with shì
tips.b: shì joins the person to the job and nothing stands where English puts a or an: tā shì jīnglǐ.

phrases.e: are you able to help me

tips.b: èr is the number two in counting and in larger numbers. In front of a measure word the form is liǎng: liǎng gè rén, liǎng bēi chá.
bǎi, qiān and wàn follow the digit that counts them: sān bǎi, wǔ qiān. Mandarin groups large numbers in ten thousands, so wàn is one unit where English needs two words.
dì in front of a number gives the position in a series, and a measure word still follows: dì-yī gè, dì-sān běn.

phrases.t: yī nián yǒu sānbǎi liùshíwǔ tiān
phrases.e: a year has three hundred and sixty-five days
phrases.ipa: i⁵ ni̯ɛn³⁵ i̯ou̯²¹⁴ san⁵.pai̯²¹⁴ li̯ou̯⁵¹.ʂʐ̩³⁵.u²¹⁴ tʰi̯ɛn⁵

phrases.t: zhè gè xuéxiào yǒu wǔbǎi gè xuésheng
phrases.e: this school has five hundred students
phrases.ipa: tʂɤ⁵¹ kɤ⁵¹ ɕɥɛ³⁵.ɕi̯ɑu̯⁵¹ i̯ou̯²¹⁴ u²¹⁴.pai̯²¹⁴ kɤ⁵¹ ɕɥɛ³⁵.ʂəŋ
phrases.note: 这个学校有五百个学生

phrases.t: tā shì wǒ de dì-yī gè lǎoshī
phrases.ipa: tʰa⁵ ʂʐ̩⁵¹ u̯ɔ²¹⁴ tə ti⁵¹.i⁵ kɤ⁵¹ lɑu̯²¹⁴.ʂʐ̩⁵

tips.b: The currency is written yuán and said kuài: sān kuài qián. qián may be left off once the amount is clear.
duōshao qián follows the thing being priced, in the slot where the amount belongs: zhè gè duōshao qián.
tài in front of an adjective and le at the end says the quality has gone past what is wanted: tài guì le.

phrases.e: this piece of clothing is cheap

units.title: OUT AND ABOUT
units.subtitle: Ordering a meal, buying things, and what people do for fun

tips.b: yào plus an amount plus the dish is the ordinary order: wǒ yào yì pán jiǎozi. The measure word matches the serving, so a plate takes pán and a bowl takes wǎn.
eg: a cup of tea for me
a plate of food for me

tips.h: qǐng in front of a verb
tips.b: qǐng before the verb turns an instruction into a request. gěi then takes two objects in a row, the person and the thing: qǐng gěi wǒ càidān.

phrases.t: zhè gè cài tài là le
phrases.ipa: tʂɤ⁵¹ kɤ⁵¹ tsʰai̯⁵¹ tʰai̯⁵¹ la⁵¹ lə

phrases.e: I would like a plate of dumplings

tips.h: zài before a verb marks it in progress
tips.b: The same zài that gives a place, placed in front of a verb, says the action is going on now: wǒ zài zhǎo yí gè bāo.

tips.h: The measure word can stand alone
tips.b: Once the thing is known the noun drops out and the measure word carries it: zhè jiàn, nà tiáo, liǎng gè.

phrases.t: wǒ yào mǎi yì tiáo kùzi
phrases.ipa: u̯ɔ²¹⁴ i̯ɑu̯⁵¹ mai̯²¹⁴ i⁵¹ tʰi̯ɑu̯³⁵ kʰu⁵¹.tsɹ̩

phrases.e: is there a discount on this one

phrases.t: wǒ zài zhǎo yí gè bāo
phrases.e: I am looking for a bag
phrases.ipa: u̯ɔ²¹⁴ tsai̯⁵¹ tʂɑu̯²¹⁴ i³⁵ kɤ⁵¹ pɑu̯⁵

tips.h: A verb that carries its own object
tips.b: chànggē is sing-song and tiàowǔ is dance-dance: the object is already inside the word. To add a count the pair splits, as in chàng yì shǒu gē.

tips.h: xǐhuan takes a noun or a verb
tips.b: What is liked may be a thing or an action, and the two forms are built the same way: wǒ xǐhuan yīnyuè, wǒ xǐhuan tīng yīnyuè.

phrases.e: we watch films at the weekend

tips.h: dǎ and tī pick the body part
tips.b: A ball played with the hands takes dǎ, and one played with the feet takes tī: dǎ lánqiú, tī zúqiú. Swimming and running are single verbs and take neither.
huì asks whether the skill has been learned and xǐhuan asks about taste, so the two questions get different answers.

phrases.e: there is a match this evening

units.title: THE WORLD
units.subtitle: Landscape, the city, countries and languages, and more verbs

tips.b: The place comes first, then yǒu, then what stands in it: shān shàngmiàn yǒu shù. English begins with there is, which reverses the order.
eg: there are trees on the mountain
there is a cat at home

tips.h: hěn duō for a large amount
tips.b: duō in front of a noun does not stand alone; hěn duō is the ordinary way to say many or much: hěn duō huā.

phrases.e: there are trees on the mountain

phrases.t: gōngyuán lǐmiàn yǒu hěn duō huā
phrases.e: there are many flowers in the park
phrases.ipa: kʊŋ⁵.ɥɛn³⁵ li²¹⁴.mi̯ɛn⁵¹ i̯ou̯²¹⁴ xən²¹⁴ tu̯ɔ⁵ xu̯a⁵

phrases.e: the stars can be seen at night

tips.b: cóng gives where a movement begins and dào where it ends, and both stand before the verb: cóng jiā dào gōngsī.
After a place the position word often keeps only its first syllable: chéngshì lǐ, zhuōzi shàng. The longer lǐmiàn and shàngmiàn are equally correct.

phrases.e: the museum is behind the square

phrases.t: chéngshì lǐmiàn yǒu hěn duō lóu
phrases.e: there are many buildings in the city
phrases.ipa: tʂʰəŋ³⁵.ʂʐ̩⁵¹ li²¹⁴.mi̯ɛn⁵¹ i̯ou̯²¹⁴ xən²¹⁴ tu̯ɔ⁵ lou̯³⁵

tips.h: A nationality is country plus rén
tips.b: No separate adjective exists: Zhōngguó rén, Měiguó rén. The question uses nǎ in the same slot: nǐ shì nǎ guó rén.
guó names the country, and wén or yǔ names its language: Zhōngguó and zhōngwén, Yīngguó and yīngwén. Both language endings are used, wén more often in writing.

phrases.e: I can speak a little English

tips.h: A doubled verb softens the action
tips.b: Saying the verb twice makes it short and casual: kànkan, děngdeng, shuōshuo. The meaning is the same action, done briefly.
yíxià follows the verb for the same effect and is more common in speech: děng yíxià, kàn yíxià.

tips.h: Where the object of a request goes
tips.b: gěi, sòng and jièshào take the person first and the thing second, in that fixed order: gěi wǒ shū, sòng tā huā.

phrases.t: nǐ kěyǐ yòng wǒ de diànnǎo
phrases.ipa: ni²¹⁴ kʰɤ²¹⁴.i²¹⁴ i̯ʊŋ⁵¹ u̯ɔ²¹⁴ tə ti̯ɛn⁵¹.nɑu̯²¹⁴
